title: Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling
subtitle: Watch one overloaded server get fixed two ways, a bigger box or more boxes, and see what each choice costs.
learn: The difference between scaling up (vertical) and scaling out (horizontal)
Why a single big machine has both a hard ceiling and a single point of failure
How adding servers behind a load balancer raises capacity and survives failures
Why cost per request served often rises at the top of the instance range
When a bigger box is the right and simplest answer, especially for databases

steps.title: One server is running hot
steps.body: Picture your shop on one server with 4 vCPUs (CPU cores). For this lesson we assume it can handle about 800 requests per second, and it costs about $150 a month. Traffic has doubled and now peaks at 680, so the CPU is 85 percent busy (680 out of 800). That is risky: delays start to grow well before 100 percent, and one more busy week would cause queues and timeouts. You have two basic fixes: a bigger machine, or more machines.
steps.idea: To fix a capacity problem you either make the machine bigger or add more machines.
steps.caption: 680 req/s are arriving at a server that tops out at 800.

steps.title: Scale up: a bigger box
steps.body: Scale up means swapping in a bigger machine: more CPU cores, more RAM, faster disks. The animation sends the same 680 requests per second to one 16 vCPU server. Its capacity rises to about 2,800 requests per second (a bit under 4x, because busy cores get in each other's way), so CPU drops to 24 percent. At these sizes the cloud price grows roughly with size, so the bill goes from $150 to about $600 a month. Your code does not change at all.
steps.idea: Scaling up is the simplest fix because the application stays exactly the same.
steps.caption: The same traffic now lands on one much larger server.

steps.title: The limits of one machine
steps.body: Keep growing the single machine and you hit walls. Imagine a 64 vCPU server: about 9,000 requests per second, not the 12,800 you would expect from 16 times the cores, because cores slow each other down. It costs about $2,400 a month, so every request you serve gets more expensive. Resizing usually needs a restart. Worst of all, it is still one machine: if it dies, the whole site is down. That is called a single point of failure (SPOF).
steps.idea: Scaling up has a hard ceiling, a rising cost per request, and no protection if the machine fails.
steps.caption: Even a 64 vCPU box is one crash away from an outage.

steps.title: Scale out: more boxes
steps.body: Scale out means adding more ordinary machines and sharing the work between them. Now a load balancer (a traffic director) sits in front of three 4 vCPU servers and sends each request to one of them. Together they handle about 2,400 requests per second, for roughly $450 of servers plus $20 for the balancer. Need more later? Add a fourth server for another 800. The catch: your app must work no matter which server answers.
steps.idea: Scale out adds capacity in small steps by putting ordinary machines behind a load balancer.
steps.caption: A load balancer now spreads requests over three servers.

steps.title: Work is shared
steps.body: The 680 requests per second are split three ways, about 227 per server, so each server is only about 28 percent busy. All three read and write the same database, which is where shared data lives. This only works if servers keep no personal user data in their own memory. Otherwise the next request might reach a server that has never met that user. The stateless lesson covers that fix, and the load balancing lesson covers the sharing rules.
steps.idea: Scale out works when any server can handle any request, so user data must live outside the servers.
steps.caption: Each server gets about a third of the traffic; all share one database.

steps.title: One server dies
steps.body: Now server 2 crashes. The load balancer's health checks (small regular test requests) notice, and it stops sending traffic there. The two survivors can still handle about 1,600 requests per second, far above your 680, so each takes 340 and sits at about 43 percent CPU. Users barely notice, apart from a few failed requests before detection. Keeping spare capacity beyond your peak, called N+1, turns a hardware failure into a non-event. The single big server could not do this.
steps.idea: Many small servers survive failures, and spare capacity is what makes that survival real.
steps.caption: Server 2 fails; the other two split its traffic.

steps.title: What scale out costs you
steps.body: Scaling out moves the difficulty from hardware to software and operations. You now need a load balancer, health checks, deployment to many machines, and monitoring for all of them. Each added server also adds some overhead, so gains are slightly under linear. The bigger issue is the database. The app tier can now take 3 times the traffic, but all servers share one database, and each server keeps its own pool of open database connections. More servers means more connections, and a database has a connection limit. Splitting data is much harder than adding stateless servers.
steps.idea: Scaling out adds complexity, and the shared database becomes the next bottleneck.
steps.caption: Three servers all feed one database, which is nearing its connection limit.

steps.title: When the bigger box wins
steps.body: A relational database is the classic case for scaling up. It keeps data consistent in one place, and splitting it across machines is hard. So the usual first move is a bigger instance with more RAM, so frequently used data stays in memory, which is fast. Small products also do well with one box: at 680 requests per second, one mid-size server, maybe with a standby, is simpler to run than a fleet. Scale up first while it is cheap and easy, then scale out when you hit the ceiling or need failure tolerance.
steps.idea: Scale up first for databases and small systems; scale out when you need failure tolerance or outgrow one box.
steps.caption: Make the database bigger first; its hot data stays in RAM.

steps.title: Pick by the constraint
steps.body: Scaling up is simple and needs no code change, but it has a ceiling, a rising cost per request at the top, and one point of failure. Scaling out adds capacity in small steps and survives failures, but needs stateless servers, a load balancer, and a plan for shared data. Most real systems do both: they scale the database up first (adding read replicas, extra copies used for reading, later) and scale the stateless app servers out.
steps.idea: Scale up for simplicity, scale out for headroom and resilience, and combine them.
steps.caption: Both paths side by side: one big box, or a pool of servers.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes the main weakness of scaling up a single server, even a very large one?
options: It always requires rewriting the application
It has a hard ceiling and remains a single point of failure
It cannot use more than 4 CPU cores
It makes the database slower by definition
quiz.why: A bigger box needs no code change, but there is a largest machine you can buy, and if that one machine fails everything it serves goes down.

quiz.q: You run three servers, each at 75 percent CPU at peak. One fails. What is the most likely result?
options: Nothing changes because load balancers add capacity
The other two run near 90 percent, which is tight but workable
The other two need about 112 percent each, so they overload and requests fail
The failed server's traffic is automatically dropped
quiz.why: Three servers at 75 percent carry 2.25 servers' worth of work. Two servers can only supply 2.0, so they cannot keep up. This is why N+1 headroom matters: size the fleet so peak load still fits after losing one.

quiz.q: Your stateless web tier is at its limit and you must keep serving if one machine fails; your single database is at 40 percent CPU with room to spare. What is the sensible first move?
options: Add more web servers behind the load balancer
Shard the database across four servers
Replace the web tier with one very large server
Switch the database to a different vendor
quiz.why: Several stateless servers give more capacity and survive a single failure; one big server would still be a single point of failure, and the database has headroom so sharding adds complexity for nothing.

quiz.q: A team wants to scale a primary relational database for the next year with minimal risk. Why is a larger instance often a good first choice?
options: Databases cannot run on more than one machine ever
Bigger instances are always cheaper per core
Scaling out is impossible in the cloud
It keeps data in one place with no new consistency problems and needs no application changes
quiz.why: A single primary avoids splitting data and the coordination problems that follow. Scaling up is often the simplest path until you outgrow it, though replicas and sharding exist for later.

cheatsheet.def: Make one machine bigger with more CPU, RAM, or faster disks. Simple, no code change, but has a ceiling and one point of failure.
Add more machines and spread work across them. Grows in small steps and tolerates failures, but needs stateless design and a load balancer.
A component whose failure takes the whole system down. One big server is the typical example.
Keep enough spare capacity that losing any one server still leaves you above peak load. A rule of thumb, not a guarantee.
Cloud price per vCPU is roughly linear with size, but capacity gains flatten at the top, so cost per request rises. Specialty and on-prem top-end hardware can also cost more per core.
Scale up first while it is cheap and simple. Scale out the stateless tier when you need headroom or resilience. Scale databases out last (read replicas first, sharding last).
